capitals.name: Langzhou (Changde)
capitals.note: power was usually centred at Lang Prefecture (modern Changde) during the years of de facto independence; Tanzhou (Changsha) was the Chu capital and the Southern Tang's seat until 1 December 952. Coordinates are the modern city's.

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe (Cliopatria has no Wuping row; its Southern Chu shape runs to 959 and covers Hunan and the Guangxi prefectures). In 952 Chu generals rose and expelled the Southern Tang expeditionary force but Tanzhou stayed Southern Tang until 1 December 952, so only the Langzhou country is drawn as Wuping's core until the ledger's December gain. The core is the researcher's reading.

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. The page gives Ma Chu 'present-day Hunan and northeastern Guangxi' and no area; modern Hunan is about 212,000 km2 against Cliopatria's 416,000 km2 for Southern Chu 947-959, a ratio near 0.5, because the Guangxi prefectures are left out (the Southern Tang page records a Southern Han invasion of Lingnan in winter 951; the Ma Chu page is silent on Guangxi after 951). The Wuping circuit is drawn as Hunan only.

ledger.note: 952: Chu generals rise and the Wuping circuit begins. In 952 Chu generals rose against the Southern Tang and expelled its expeditionary force, and the former Chu territory was then ruled by a series of generals holding the Wuping Jiedushi title (the page, paraphrased). The page gives no month and no boundary; the Langzhou country as core is the researcher's reading of power was usually centred at Lang Prefecture (modern Changde).

ledger.note: 1 December 952: Hunan passes from the Southern Tang to the former Chu generals. Bian Hao fled Tanzhou on 1 December 952 and Liu Yan 'submitted to the Later Zhou in order to protect against a potentially revanchist Southern Tang'. Matches southern-tang's loss of Hunan on the same day; the Wuping name is the Ma Chu page's.

region.text: the former Chu territory ('present-day Hunan and northeastern Guangxi' for the Ma Chu; the Wuping circuit held its Hunan part)

ledger.note: 963: the Song seize Hunan and the Wuping circuit ends. In 963 the Wuping Jiedushi ended and the Song dynasty seized its territory (the page, paraphrased). Gao Jichong's page: Zhou Xingfeng died in 962 leaving Zhou Baoquan, a general (Zhang Wenbiao of Hengzhou) rebelled, and the Song army 'passing through the Jingnan' took Jiangling on the way; the page names no battle in Hunan and no month. northern-song's ledger records the same gain with Jingnan as counterpart.

wars.name: Southern Tang conquest of Chu and the Hunan rebellion

zones.text: the former Chu territory ('present-day Hunan and northeastern Guangxi' for the Ma Chu; the Wuping circuit held its Hunan part)

wars.outcome: The Southern Tang subjugated Chu in 951, but 'much of the state was lost in a rebellion against the deeply unpopular Southern Tang administration'; Bian Hao fled Tanzhou on 1 December 952 and Hunan passed to the former Chu generals.
wars.note: The page has no separate war article; the 951 phase belongs to southern-chu's and southern-tang's dossiers.

wars.name: Song campaign against Jingnan and Wuping
wars.outcome: The Song army, sent against Zhang Wenbiao's rebellion in Wuping, took Jiangling without a fight and the Wuping Jiedushi was ended in 963.
wars.note: Zones left empty: the page names no engagement in Hunan, so no contest is drawn for 963.

certainty.note: No boundary is recorded: Hunan's modern outline stands for the circuit; the Guangxi side and the Jingnan frontier are not given by any page opened.

notes: Written by g-ea (gap batch) on 2026-11-01 from four pages. The page 'Wuping Circuit' does not exist on English Wikipedia (url_not_found), so wikipedia is null; the Ma Chu article carries the story. The pages show the regime less unified than 'one state' suggests: after Liu Yan's rising Wang Kui captured Langzhou and (according to the Pan Shusi page) sent Pan Shusi to execute Liu Yan, Mo Hongwan held Tan Prefecture and named his army the Wuping army, Pan Shusi killed Wang Kui in February 956, and Zhou Xingfeng entered Langzhou in 956 and ruled until his death in 962; none of these moves is dated closely enough to draw. No continuous ruler list exists in the pages (Liu Yan 952, Wang Kui, Zhou Xingfeng 956-962, Zhou Baoquan 962-963), so identity.rulers is omitted. Nominal allegiance (Liu Yan 'submitted to the Later Zhou'; later the Song) is not drawn as a vassalage: the Ma Chu page calls the years de facto independence and no page dates a change of overlord. The Guangxi part of Ma Chu (Gui, Wuzhou prefectures) is outside this dossier: the Southern Tang page says the Southern Han invaded Lingnan in winter 951 and the Ma Chu page is silent after 951; a gap-filler should settle who held Guilin and Wuzhou 951-963. northern-song's ledger line 1 (963 gain of Jingnan and Hunan) names jingnan as the counterpart for Hunan; it should name wuping-circuit for the Hunan part.
